clinicalPearls: The classic clinical triad is progressive sensorineural hearing loss, cerebellar ataxia and, later, myelopathy, evolving slowly over years
Results from chronic, repeated low-grade bleeding into the subarachnoid space with deposition of haemosiderin on the pial surfaces of the brain, brainstem, cerebellum, cranial nerves and spinal cord
The eighth cranial nerve and cerebellum are especially vulnerable, explaining the early prominence of hearing loss and ataxia
Susceptibility-weighted or gradient-echo MRI shows a characteristic rim of low signal (haemosiderin) coating the surface of the neuraxis
A meticulous search for the bleeding source is essential and may reveal a dural defect, prior trauma or surgery, a vascular lesion or a tumour
Anosmia and cognitive change can accompany the core triad in some patients
The infratentorial (classic) form differs from cortical superficial siderosis, which is more typically associated with cerebral amyloid angiopathy
reference.pathophysiology: Superficial siderosis of the central nervous system arises from persistent or recurrent haemorrhage into the subarachnoid space, releasing blood that breaks down to deposit haemosiderin along the pial and subpial surfaces of the neuraxis. Iron-laden macrophages and free iron promote oxidative injury and the accumulation of ferritin and haemosiderin in tissues rich in Bergmann glia and microglia, which accounts for the particular vulnerability of the cerebellum and the eighth cranial nerve. Progressive neuronal and glial damage produces the characteristic sensorineural deafness, cerebellar ataxia and myelopathy. Identifying and treating the chronic source of bleeding, such as a dural tear, is central to halting progression.
additionalDifferentials: Vestibular schwannoma or other causes of sensorineural hearing loss
Multiple sclerosis or other causes of progressive ataxia and myelopathy
Cerebral amyloid angiopathy causing cortical superficial siderosis
Spinocerebellar ataxias and other hereditary ataxias
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the whole neuraxis with susceptibility-weighted or gradient-echo sequences to demonstrate haemosiderin deposition
Dedicated spinal imaging and CT myelography to identify a dural defect or cerebrospinal fluid leak
Audiometry to characterise sensorineural hearing loss
Cerebrospinal fluid analysis, which may show xanthochromia or evidence of prior bleeding
Vascular imaging to exclude an underlying vascular malformation or aneurysm
Imaging for an occult tumour as a potential bleeding source
redFlags: Progressive myelopathy with gait and sphincter deterioration
An identifiable and potentially treatable bleeding source such as a dural defect
Rapidly worsening hearing loss threatening communication
Features suggesting an underlying tumour or vascular malformation
reference.prognosis: Superficial siderosis is usually slowly progressive, and neurological deficits such as hearing loss and ataxia are often irreversible; identifying and repairing the bleeding source may arrest further deterioration, so prognosis depends heavily on early recognition and treatment of the cause.
pitfalls: Failing to search thoroughly for the chronic bleeding source, including a spinal dural defect
Confusing infratentorial superficial siderosis with cortical siderosis of cerebral amyloid angiopathy
Attributing hearing loss and ataxia to ageing or unrelated causes and missing the imaging signature
Assuming the condition is untreatable and not pursuing a correctable dural or vascular lesion
references: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
management: Identify and surgically repair the chronic source of subarachnoid bleeding, such as a dural defect or cerebrospinal fluid leak, to arrest progression
Consider the CNS-penetrant iron chelator deferiprone to reduce haemosiderin deposition
Provide hearing rehabilitation with hearing aids, and cochlear implantation for advanced sensorineural deafness
Offer physiotherapy and vestibular rehabilitation for cerebellar ataxia and gait impairment
Monitor disease with serial susceptibility-weighted or gradient-echo MRI and audiometry
Coordinate care across neurology, neurosurgery, ENT and audiology, and renew the search for a bleeding source if deterioration continues
